groups.high: An electric vehicle lithium-ion battery can undergo thermal runaway: internal reactions generate heat and flammable gases, potentially propagating between cells. Extinguishing visible flames does not necessarily stop this process. Dry chemical or carbon dioxide extinguishers can suppress some external flames but may provide insufficient cooling inside a damaged pack. Fire crews may require sustained water application and thousands of gallons; 3,000 gallons is not a universal minimum, and neither a fixed cooling time nor a single temperature guarantees safety. Manufacturer emergency-response guidance and incident conditions determine tactics. Responders must consider high-voltage components, toxic smoke, access to the battery, exposure protection, and possible delayed reignition during transport or storage. Water is an important cooling tool, not a claim that every incident has only one acceptable tactic. A bystander should move away, keep others back, avoid smoke, and call emergency services from a safe place. Do not open, pierce, move, or attempt to cool a burning battery pack yourself. A vehicle that appears extinguished still requires trained assessment and appropriate isolation.
groups.mid: An electric vehicle's lithium-ion battery can enter thermal runaway. Reactions inside it make more heat and gas that can burn. The damage can spread from cell to cell. Putting out the flames may not stop what is happening inside. A dry chemical or carbon dioxide extinguisher may put out some outside flames without cooling the pack enough. Fire crews may need a steady water supply and thousands of gallons. But 3,000 gallons is not a fixed minimum for every fire, and a set time or temperature cannot prove the pack is safe. Crews use the maker's emergency guide and assess the scene. They must consider high voltage, toxic smoke, access to the battery, nearby people, and the risk that fire starts again during moving or storage. Water helps cool the pack, but tactics depend on the incident. If you are nearby, move away, keep others back, avoid the smoke, and call emergency services from safety. Do not open, pierce, or move a burning pack. Do not try to cool it yourself. Even after the fire seems out, trained crews must check and isolate the vehicle.
groups.low: An electric vehicle battery can get so hot that reactions inside it make still more heat. This is thermal runaway. It can make gas that burns and spread from cell to cell. The flames may stop while heat remains inside, and a dry chemical or carbon dioxide extinguisher may put out outside flames without cooling the battery enough. Fire crews may need to use water for a long time. They may need thousands of gallons, but not every fire needs at least 3,000. A fixed time or heat level cannot prove safety. Crews must check the scene and the maker's emergency guide while they watch for high voltage, toxic smoke, access problems, and harm to people nearby. The fire may start again when the vehicle is moved or stored. Water is useful for cooling, but the safest plan depends on the fire. If you are nearby, move away, keep others back, and stay out of the smoke. Call emergency services from a safe place. Do not open or pierce the pack, move it, or try to cool it yourself. A trained crew must check the vehicle and keep it safely apart even if the flames seem out.
groups.source_review: Checked NFPA incident discussion and manufacturer response guide hosted by NFPA. Not a firefighter operating procedure.
groups.notes: Removed fabricated NFPA standard citations, fixed water/time/temperature requirements, and water-only universal claim.

groups.high: Methane mixed with air is flammable at approximately 5–15% methane by volume under ordinary conditions. The lower explosive limit, or LEL, is about 5% methane, not 5% of the LEL. Workplace alarms and evacuation thresholds can be set well below that concentration. A suspected leak requires prompt withdrawal rather than waiting for a dangerous reading. Avoid flames, sparks, electrical switches, and ordinary phones or radios within the suspected gas area. Do not turn equipment off or start fans if doing so could create an ignition source. Move to a safe location and contact emergency services or the gas utility there. Ordinary mobile phones are not generally explosion-proof; hazardous-area equipment needs appropriate certification and procedures. Methane may also displace oxygen, and gas distribution can vary with ventilation and enclosure geometry. Do not re-enter, investigate, or attempt a rescue in the hazardous area without authorization, training, and suitable equipment. Professionals must isolate the source, assess ventilation, and verify safe conditions. A reading above the upper flammable limit is not safe, since dilution can create a flammable mixture.
groups.mid: Methane can burn or explode when it makes up about 5–15% of air under ordinary conditions. The lower explosive limit, or LEL, is about 5% methane. That is not the same as 5% of the LEL. Workplace alarms may sound at much lower levels. If you suspect a gas leak, leave at once rather than waiting for a dangerous reading. Do not use flames, switches, or normal phones and radios in the gas area. Do not switch machines off or start fans if that could cause a spark. Get to a safe place, then call emergency services or the gas company. A normal mobile phone is not usually explosion-proof. Special equipment needs the right safety rating and rules. Methane can also push oxygen out of the air. The amount of gas may differ from place to place. Do not go back, look for the leak, or try a rescue without the right training, gear, and permission. Experts must stop the source, assess airflow, and check safety. Even gas above the upper limit is unsafe: adding air can make it explosive.
groups.low: If you think gas is leaking, leave now. Do not wait for a test. Methane can burn or explode at about 5–15% in air. The low end, about 5%, is called the LEL. This is not 5% of the LEL. An alarm may sound well before this. Stay away from flames and sparks. Do not use a light switch. Do not use a phone or radio near the leak. Do not turn machines off or fans on if this could make a spark. Go to a safe place. Call for help from there. Call emergency services or the gas firm. Most phones are not explosion-proof. Special gear needs the right safety rating and rules. Methane can leave too little oxygen to breathe. Gas levels can vary round a room. Do not go back to find the leak. Do not try to rescue someone in the gas area unless you have the right training, gear, and permission. Experts must stop the leak and check the air. Too much gas is not safe either. If air mixes with it, it may burn or explode.
groups.source_review: Checked OSHA gas-line emergency advice and NIOSH/OSHA methane flammability table.
groups.notes: Replaced unsafe switch-off/ventilation-first advice with leave-and-call-from-safety; corrected concentration/LEL confusion and phone certification claim.

groups.high: If an elevator stalls, remain inside, use the alarm or emergency communication system, and report the location, occupants, and any urgent medical or smoke hazard. Follow instructions from the dispatcher and trained rescuers. Do not force doors, jump, climb through a ceiling hatch, or attempt to cross into the shaft. A car may be between floors or move unexpectedly, making self-extraction dangerous. Elevator brakes, interlocks, and other protective systems are designed to reduce risk, but their presence does not guarantee that a particular stalled car is secure. A quoted 125% load figure can relate to particular code tests or equipment requirements; it is not universal proof of brake capacity or permission to overload. The posted rated capacity remains the operating limit. Building staff should contact the authorized elevator service or emergency responders rather than attempt an improvised rescue. If communication fails, use another available means to summon help without manipulating equipment. Rescue should be performed by personnel who can secure the system and assess its condition.
groups.mid: If an elevator stops and will not move, stay inside and use its alarm or emergency phone. Tell the dispatcher where you are, who is inside, and whether anyone is ill or there is smoke. Follow the instructions you receive. Do not force the doors, jump, climb through the roof hatch, or step into the shaft. The car may be between floors and could move without warning. Brakes and door locks help keep people safe, but they do not prove that this stalled car is secure. You may hear that brakes hold 125% of the rated load. Such a number may come from a particular test or equipment rule. It is not a promise for every lift, or a reason to exceed the posted weight limit. Building staff should call the authorized lift service or emergency responders instead of trying a rescue themselves. If the emergency phone fails, use another safe way to call for help without touching the machinery. Trained rescuers must secure and check the lift before getting people out.
groups.low: If a lift stops, stay inside and use the alarm or emergency phone to say where you are and who is with you. Tell them if someone is ill or you see smoke. Follow their advice. Do not force the doors or jump. Do not climb through the roof hatch or step into the lift shaft. The car may not be level with a floor and could move when you do not expect it. Brakes and door locks help protect you, but they do not prove this lift is secure. A claim about holding 125% of the load may refer to a certain test or part, not a promise for every lift. Keep to the weight limit on the sign. Building staff should call the approved lift service or emergency crews, not try a rescue themselves. If the phone does not work, use another safe way to call for help. Do not touch the machinery, since trained crews must make the lift secure and check it before helping you out.
groups.source_review: Checked manufacturer owner's guide for passenger entrapment and trained-rescue advice. Full ASME code not independently accessed; 125% not certified as universal.
groups.notes: Removed universal brake guarantee and implication of extra permitted load.

groups.high: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hypochlorite, the active ingredient in many bleach products, are incompatible. Mixing them can release toxic chlorine gas and cause serious lung injury. Store them in separate, compatible containment arrangements so that leaks, shared drains, or handling mistakes cannot bring them together. Follow each product's Safety Data Sheet, particularly handling and storage, exposure controls, and stability and reactivity information. OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200, requires hazard communication through labels, accessible SDSs, and worker training; it does not establish a universal ten-foot separation rule for these chemicals. Required distance, barriers, ventilation, and containment depend on products, quantities, facility conditions, and applicable rules. A wall alone is insufficient if spills can mix around it. Keep containers closed and correctly labeled; never transfer chemicals into unmarked containers or mix cleaners. If a release occurs, leave the affected area, keep others away, and obtain emergency assistance. Do not attempt cleanup or neutralization without appropriate training and protection. Breathing difficulty after exposure requires urgent medical assessment.
groups.mid: Keep hydrochloric acid away from sodium hypochlorite, the chemical in many bleach products. Mixing them can release chlorine gas, which can badly harm the lungs. Store them so leaks cannot meet, including through a shared drain. Use separate storage and spill containers suited to each chemical. Check the product's Safety Data Sheet, or SDS. It explains safe handling, storage, protective measures, and what reacts with the product. OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200, requires labels, access to SDSs, and worker training. It does not set a ten-foot gap for every acid-and-bleach store. The right distance, barriers, airflow, and spill control depend on the products, amounts, site, and local rules. A wall is not enough if spills can flow around it. Keep containers closed with clear labels, and never put chemicals in an unmarked bottle or mix cleaners. If gas escapes, leave, keep others away, and call for emergency help. Do not clean or neutralize the spill unless trained and properly protected. Get urgent medical help for breathing trouble after exposure.
groups.low: Do not mix hydrochloric acid with sodium hypochlorite. Sodium hypochlorite is in many bleach products, and mixing them can make chlorine gas. This gas can badly hurt your lungs. Store the products apart so leaks cannot meet. A shared drain can let spills mix too. Use separate storage and spill trays made for each product. Read its Safety Data Sheet, or SDS. This tells you how to store and handle it, what protection you need, and what reacts with it. OSHA rule 29 CFR 1910.1200 requires labels, SDS access, and staff training. It does not say every store must use a ten-foot gap. The safe gap, barriers, airflow, and spill controls depend on the product, amount, site, and rules. A wall will not help if spills flow round it. Keep lids shut and labels clear. Do not use an unmarked bottle or mix cleaners. If gas escapes, leave the area and keep others out. Call for emergency help. Do not clean or treat the spill unless trained and protected. Get urgent medical help if exposure makes it hard to breathe.
groups.source_review: Checked OSHA hazard communication, SDS sections, and reported chlorine release.
groups.notes: Corrected invented mandatory ten-foot rule and absolute barrier protection.

groups.high: Radiation protection limits depend on jurisdiction, worker category, and dose quantity. Under US NRC rules, an adult worker's annual total effective dose equivalent limit is 50 mSv, or 5 rem. International IAEA standards generally specify an effective dose of 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years, with 50 mSv in any single year. These are limits, not targets or assurances of zero cancer risk; exposure should also be optimized below them. Additional limits apply to particular organs and special groups. The sievert measures biologically weighted dose, whereas the gray measures absorbed energy per mass; they are not universally interchangeable. An acute whole-body dose near 4 Gy can be life-threatening, but an LD50 value depends on radiation type, exposure distribution, observation period, and treatment. It is not a precise universal LD50/30 or an individual prediction. Annual low-dose exposure cannot be directly equated with a short, intense whole-body exposure. Suspected major exposure needs emergency medical and radiation-specialist assessment. Treatment and prognosis depend on measured findings, not a simple comparison with the occupational limit.
groups.mid: Radiation limits depend on the country, type of worker, and kind of dose. US NRC rules limit an adult worker's total effective dose equivalent to 50 mSv, or 5 rem, per year. IAEA standards generally use an effective dose of 20 mSv a year averaged over five years, with no more than 50 mSv in one year. These are upper limits. Do not aim to reach them. They do not mean there is no cancer risk, so exposure should be kept lower where reasonably possible. There are extra limits for some organs and groups. A sievert describes a dose weighted for its biological effects. A gray describes energy absorbed per mass. You cannot always swap the units. A sudden whole-body dose near 4 Gy can threaten life. But the dose that kills half a group, called LD50, varies with radiation type, body area, time followed, and treatment. A fixed LD50/30 does not predict one person's outcome. A small dose spread over a year is not the same as a large dose in minutes. If major exposure is suspected, seek emergency medical and radiation-expert assessment. Findings guide care, not a simple comparison with a work limit.
groups.low: Radiation limits are not the same everywhere. They depend on the country, worker, and kind of dose. US NRC rules set an adult worker's yearly limit at 50 mSv, or 5 rem, for total effective dose equivalent. IAEA rules generally use 20 mSv a year on average over five years, with at most 50 mSv in one year. These are limits, not goals. They do not mean there is no cancer risk. Keep doses lower where reasonably possible. Some organs and groups have extra limits. A sievert weighs dose for its effects on the body. A gray measures energy absorbed per mass. The units cannot always be swapped. A sudden dose near 4 Gy to the whole body may be fatal. LD50 means a dose that kills half an exposed group. It changes with radiation type, body area, time followed, and care. A fixed LD50/30 is not a sure rule or a forecast for one person. A dose spread over a year is not the same as a high dose in minutes. If a major exposure may have happened, get emergency care and radiation-expert help. Tests and findings guide treatment, not a work-limit comparison alone.
groups.source_review: Checked NRC annual limit, IAEA five-year rule, and CDC acute-radiation guidance.
groups.notes: Corrected annual/career limit confusion, universal mSv-to-Gy conversion, exact LD50/30 and unsupported individual risk/treatment claims.

groups.high: Grid frequency reflects the balance between generation and demand in a synchronous electricity system. In a nominal 50 Hz grid, insufficient generation tends to lower frequency; excess generation tends to raise it. A change of 1–2 Hz equals 2–4% of 50 Hz, but this arithmetic is not a universal relay-setting standard. Protection thresholds and time delays depend on the grid, equipment, and applicable coordination rules. Governors, reserves, storage, and other frequency responses can restore balance. Under-frequency load shedding disconnects selected demand to preserve the remaining system. Generator protection may disconnect a machine outside its safe operating envelope; doing so removes generation, not demand, and can worsen an existing shortage. Coordinated settings therefore seek to avoid unnecessary trips while protecting equipment. Multiple losses can create a cascade and a blackout, but one frequency deviation does not make that outcome inevitable. Thermal overloading of a line and system-wide frequency imbalance are related but distinct problems. IEEE, NERC, and IEC documents have specific scopes and jurisdictions; NERC requirements should not be presented as a universal 50 Hz rule. Operational intervention belongs to qualified grid personnel.
groups.mid: In a 50 Hz power grid, frequency helps show whether supply matches demand. Too little generation tends to make frequency fall; too much tends to make it rise. A change of 1–2 Hz is 2–4% of 50 Hz. That does not mean every safety relay must trip at that point. Its limits and delay depend on the grid, equipment, and rules. Generator controls, spare power, storage, and other responses can bring supply and demand back into balance. Under-frequency load shedding cuts off selected demand to protect the rest of the grid. A generator's own protection may shut it off if conditions become unsafe. That removes supply, not demand, and may make a shortage worse. Safety settings must therefore work together, keeping machines safe without needless shutdowns. Several failures may lead to a wider blackout, but a single frequency change does not guarantee one. Too much current heating a line is not exactly the same problem as frequency falling across the grid. IEEE, NERC, and IEC documents apply to defined equipment and places. NERC rules are not a single worldwide rule for 50 Hz grids. Only qualified grid staff should make operating changes.
groups.low: A power grid needs supply to match demand, and in a 50 Hz grid, frequency tends to fall if there is too little power. It tends to rise if there is too much. A change of 1–2 Hz is 2–4% of 50 Hz. This is not one fixed trip rule for all grids. Safety relays have limits and delays set for the grid and its machines. Spare power, storage, and generator controls can help restore balance. One safety method cuts power to some users. It is called under-frequency load shedding. It cuts demand to help the rest of the grid. A generator may also shut off to protect itself. This cuts supply, not demand. It can make a power shortage worse. The safety settings must work together to avoid needless trips while protecting machines. A chain of losses can cause a blackout, but one frequency change need not do so. A line getting too hot from current is a different issue from low grid frequency. The issues may be linked. IEEE, NERC, and IEC rules have their own scopes and places. NERC is not one worldwide 50 Hz rule. Qualified grid staff must handle operating changes.
groups.source_review: Checked NERC protection-coordination and load-shedding material. No equipment-specific setpoints prescribed.
groups.notes: Corrected false claim that tripping generators reduces demand, invented universal 1–2 Hz setting, and misplaced NERC/IEC scope.

groups.high: Bridge limits distinguish gross vehicle mass, individual axle loads, axle spacing, and sometimes vehicle configurations. A 40–44-tonne figure can describe a permitted whole vehicle in particular jurisdictions, not a universal single-axle allowance. A posted bridge restriction can be lower than a general road limit. Overloading raises stresses and can damage decks, joints, bearings, and structural members. Repeated stress cycles can initiate or extend fatigue cracks, with life depending on detail, material, corrosion, load spectrum, and existing damage. In a simplified stress-life model where life is inversely proportional to stress range raised to a power of three to five, a 26% stress increase gives approximately 50% to 31% of the original life, not an automatic tenfold reduction. Neither a 20% load increase nor a single crossing has a universal lifespan consequence. AASHTO and European design standards are not substitutes for local legal limits or an assessment of a particular bridge. Operators must obey posted axle and gross limits and obtain required permits. Engineers use inspection, load rating, and traffic information to decide whether monitoring, strengthening, or restriction is needed.
groups.mid: A bridge may limit the whole vehicle or each axle. Axle spacing and vehicle layout can matter too. A figure such as 40–44 tonnes may refer to the whole vehicle in some places. It is not a safe weight for one axle everywhere. A sign on a bridge may set a lower limit than the road rule. Too much weight adds stress to the deck, joints, bearings, and main supports. Repeated loads can start cracks or make them grow. This fatigue depends on the material, design detail, rust, past damage, and pattern of loads. Some models relate fatigue life to a power of stress. With a power of three to five, a 26% rise in stress gives about 50% to 31% of the old life, not a fixed tenfold drop. A 20% extra load or one crossing does not have one known effect on every bridge. AASHTO and European design rules do not replace local limits or an engineer's bridge assessment. Follow both the posted axle and whole-vehicle limits, and get permits if required. Engineers use inspections, load ratings, and traffic data to decide whether to monitor, strengthen, or restrict a bridge.
groups.low: A bridge sign may limit the weight of a whole vehicle or the weight on each axle. Axle spacing and vehicle layout can matter too. A 40–44-tonne limit may be for the whole vehicle in some places. It is not a rule that one axle may carry that much. A bridge sign can set a lower limit than the road rule. Extra weight puts more stress on the deck, joints, bearings, and main supports. Repeated loads can start cracks or make cracks grow. The result depends on the design, material, rust, past damage, and loads. Some models use a power of three to five to link stress and life. In those models, 26% more stress leaves about 50% to 31% of the old life. It does not always cut life to one tenth. An extra 20% load, or one trip across, has no fixed effect on every bridge. AASHTO and European design rules do not replace local law or a check of that bridge. Follow the axle and whole-vehicle limits on signs. Get a permit if needed. Engineers check the bridge, its load rating, and traffic before deciding on repairs, monitoring, or limits.
groups.source_review: Checked FHWA distinction between axle, gross-weight and bridge-formula limits; independently checked stated fatigue power-law arithmetic. Full AASHTO/EN provisions not certified.
groups.notes: Corrected gross-versus-axle confusion and quantitatively false tenfold fatigue claim.

groups.high: Pressure vessels require properly selected, certified pressure-relief protection matched to their maximum allowable working pressure, or MAWP, service conditions, and governing code edition. A single relief device is generally set at or below MAWP. Some ASME Section VIII arrangements permit supplemental fire-relief devices with set pressures up to 110% of MAWP, but this is a conditional code provision, not permission to raise the ordinary operating pressure. Set pressure, overpressure above the valve setting, and accumulation above vessel MAWP are different quantities. They must not be treated as the same 110% limit. Required discharge capacity, inlet and outlet losses, backpressure, fluid behavior, and fire exposure require engineering assessment. Fire can weaken the vessel wall even if pressure relief operates; a valve does not guarantee survival under every heat exposure. Corrosion and changes in service can require reassessment of vessel ratings and protection. Operators should never bypass, cap, or independently reset a relief device. Qualified personnel must use the applicable code, manufacturer documentation, inspection findings, and authorized procedures. The setting alone is not a complete vessel safety design.
groups.mid: A pressure vessel needs a suitable, certified safety valve or other relief device. Its design must match the maximum allowable working pressure, called MAWP, the service, and the code in use. A single relief device is generally set at or below MAWP. Some ASME Section VIII designs allow an extra fire-relief device set up to 110% of MAWP. This is a special rule with conditions. It does not let you raise the vessel's normal working pressure. The pressure that opens a valve, the rise above that setting, and the rise above MAWP are different measures. They are not all the same 110% limit. Engineers must check how much the valve can release, pipe losses, backpressure, the fluid, and fire exposure. A fire can weaken the vessel wall even while the valve works. The valve cannot guarantee that the vessel survives every fire. Rust or a change in use may mean the rating and protection need a fresh check. Do not block, bypass, or reset the valve yourself. Qualified staff must use the right code, maker's documents, inspections, and approved procedures. A valve setting alone is not a full safety design.
groups.low: A pressure vessel needs a proper safety valve or other relief device. It must match the vessel's safe working pressure, its use, and the code. The safe working pressure is called MAWP. A single relief device is generally set at or below it. Some ASME Section VIII designs allow an extra fire valve set up to 110% of MAWP. That rule has conditions. It does not mean you may run the vessel at a higher pressure. The point where a valve opens is its set pressure. Pressure above that point and pressure above MAWP are different things. They are not all one 110% limit. An engineer must check how much the valve releases, pipe losses, backpressure, the fluid, and fire risk. Fire can weaken the wall even if the valve works. A valve does not make every fire safe. Rust and a change in use may require new checks of the rating and protection. Do not cap, block, bypass, or reset a relief device yourself. Trained, authorized staff must use the right code and maker's guides, with inspections and approved steps. A valve setting is only one part of safety.
groups.source_review: Checked National Board MAWP guidance and manufacturer explanation of setting versus allowable accumulation. Supplemental fire-rule wording retained conditionally; current applicable full ASME edition must be reviewed by engineer.
groups.notes: Removed false explanation that 110% guarantees vessel strength and corrected set-pressure/accumulation conflation. Requires code-edition review before operational use.

groups.high: Password security depends on unpredictability, implementation, and attack conditions, not a universal requirement that every human password contain 128 bits of entropy. A uniformly random 128-bit secret has 2 to the power 128 possible values. A uniformly random six-digit PIN has one million values, or about 19.9 bits. Human choices can be more predictable. A million guesses per second would exhaust the six-digit space in one second, but actual speed depends on whether guessing is online or offline, rate limits, device controls, and password hashing. A protected device PIN cannot automatically be equated with an unthrottled stolen password hash. NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires at least 15 characters for a single-factor password and permits a lower minimum of eight when used within multifactor authentication. It emphasizes compromised-password blocklists, rate limiting, and secure salted hashing rather than mandatory character-composition rules. Use distinct passwords or passphrases, a password manager, and suitable multifactor protection or passkeys. Even a long random secret can be stolen through phishing, malware, or insecure recovery. Neither entropy nor length alone guarantees account security.
groups.mid: A strong password needs to be hard to guess, but there is no universal rule that every password must have 128 bits of entropy. Entropy measures how unpredictable a secret is. A random 128-bit secret has 2 to the power 128 possible values. A random six-digit PIN has one million, about 19.9 bits. A person may choose a PIN that is easier to guess. At one million guesses a second, all six-digit PINs could be tried in a second. But that speed is not possible in every system. It depends on online or offline access, limits on guesses, device locks, and how passwords are stored. A PIN that unlocks a protected device is not the same as a stolen hash with no guess limit. NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires 15 characters for a password used alone. It allows a minimum of eight when the password is part of multifactor authentication. It calls for blocking known weak passwords, limiting guesses, and secure salted hashing, not fixed symbol-mixing rules. Use a different password for each account, a manager, and suitable multifactor protection or passkeys. Phishing, malware, or weak account recovery can still steal a strong secret. Length or entropy alone is not enough.
groups.low: A password must be hard to guess. But not every password has to have 128 bits of entropy. Entropy means how hard a secret is to guess. A random 128-bit secret has 2 to the power 128 values. A random six-digit PIN has one million values, or about 19.9 bits. A PIN you choose may be easier to guess. At one million guesses each second, a tool could try them all in a second. But many systems do not allow that speed. Guess limits, device locks, and how the secret is stored all matter. Online and offline attacks differ. A locked device PIN is not like a stolen password hash with no guess limit. NIST SP 800-63B-4 sets a 15-character minimum for a password used alone. If used with more than one login check, it may be eight. This is multifactor authentication. The rules call for blocking weak passwords. They call for guess limits and secure salted hashing too. They do not force a mix of symbols. Use a different password for each account. A password manager can help. Use suitable extra checks or passkeys too. A fake login page, malware, or weak recovery process can still defeat a strong password. Length or entropy alone will not keep an account safe.
groups.source_review: Checked current NIST password rules and distinction between online throttling, activation secrets, and offline guessing; entropy arithmetic independently checked.
groups.notes: Corrected invented mandatory 128-bit password standard and universal sub-second PIN-cracking claim.

groups.high: A pitot-static system estimates airspeed from the difference between total pressure at the pitot inlet and static pressure. Ice, insects, debris, or covers can obstruct these sources. The indication depends on what is blocked: an inlet blockage with an open drain can drive the reading toward zero, while trapped pitot pressure can make it change with altitude rather than actual speed. A static blockage can also affect the altimeter and vertical-speed indicator. Erroneous airspeed can lead to inappropriate control inputs and loss of control; a stall occurs when critical angle of attack is exceeded, not simply because true speed is high. Air France Flight 447 crashed on 1 June 2009 after temporary airspeed inconsistencies, likely from pitot icing, autopilot disconnection, and an unrecovered stall. France's BEA led the investigation; the event should not be attributed to a fabricated Avianca 1996 hydraulic accident or a simplistic fixed-speed sequence. Prevention includes appropriate preflight inspection, unobstructed ports, and manufacturer-specified heating and maintenance. In flight, trained crews follow the aircraft-specific unreliable-airspeed procedure, including approved pitch and thrust references. A generic instruction to ignore instruments or select an alternate static source is not an adequate substitute.
groups.mid: A pitot-static system helps show airspeed by comparing total pressure at the pitot tube with static pressure. Ice, insects, debris, or a cover can block the openings. What the gauge shows depends on the blockage. If the front inlet is blocked but the drain stays open, the reading can fall toward zero. If pressure is trapped inside, the reading can change with height instead of speed. A blocked static port can affect the height and climb-rate gauges too. Wrong speed readings can lead to wrong control inputs and loss of control. A stall happens when the wing's angle of attack gets too high, not just because true speed is high. Air France Flight 447 crashed on 1 June 2009. Temporary speed differences, likely from pitot icing, led to autopilot disconnection and an unrecovered stall. France's BEA led the inquiry. This was not the invented Avianca 1996 hydraulic-failure account or a simple fixed-speed story. Prevention includes preflight checks, clear ports, and the maker's heating and maintenance rules. In flight, trained crews use that aircraft's unreliable-airspeed procedure and approved pitch and thrust settings. A general rule to ignore gauges or switch static sources is not enough.
groups.low: A plane uses pitot and static pressure to help measure airspeed. The pitot tube senses total pressure. The static port senses outside air pressure. Ice, insects, debris, or a cover can block them. The result depends on which parts are blocked. If the pitot inlet is blocked but its drain is open, speed may read near zero. If pressure is trapped, the reading may change with height, not speed. A blocked static port can affect the height and climb-rate gauges too. Wrong speed readings can lead to wrong control moves and loss of control. A wing stalls when its angle of attack is too high. High true speed alone does not cause a stall. Air France Flight 447 crashed on 1 June 2009. Its speed readings briefly disagreed, likely due to pitot ice. The autopilot went off, and the crew did not recover from a stall. France's BEA led the inquiry. The old story about an Avianca 1996 hydraulic accident was wrong. So was the simple fixed-speed account. Before flight, crews check ports and follow the maker's heat and maintenance rules. In flight, trained crews use the plane's unreliable-airspeed procedure, with its approved pitch and thrust references. Just saying to ignore gauges or change static sources is not a safe flight procedure.
groups.source_review: Checked FAA blockage effects and BEA accident account. No substitute cockpit procedure provided.
groups.notes: Corrected fabricated Avianca account, wrong investigating authority, stall physics, blockage behavior, and unsafe generic control advice.
